content.text: Soph left six open threads plus a review summary. I’ll read the matching installer code so we can talk through each point with the current behavior.

Soph’s review on [PR #2152](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2152) holds up. Copilot’s `-UseBasicParsing` comments were wrong; Soph is right that the remaining issues are real. Here is the substance.

## The actual blocker: PATH update happens after the conflict throw

This is the same nightly-plus-Scoop trap Cursor flagged. `18f7d5c19` made conflict detection look at **every** `entire` on PATH, but it did not change **when** PATH is updated.

Today the order is:

1. Snapshot `Get-EntireOnPath` while `~\.local\bin` is still **not** on `$env:Path`.
2. If anything else (Scoop shim) wins, **throw**.
3. Copy the binaries.
4. **Then** call `Add-ToUserPath`.

On the documented nightly path — Scoop stable already installed, fresh `~\.local\bin` — step 2 always fires. The new directory is never added, so a rerun fails the same way forever.

Soph’s fix is the right one: call `Add-ToUserPath` **before** the conflict check so the first hit is ours and the check becomes warn-only. With `-NoPathUpdate`, throwing is still fair, but the message should say PATH was not updated because the flag said not to.

This also bites any pre-existing `entire.exe` earlier on PATH, not just Scoop.

## Path normalization is wrong for relative / tilde `-InstallDir`

`Get-NormalizedPath` uses `[IO.Path]::GetFullPath`. In Windows PowerShell 5.1 that resolves against `[Environment]::CurrentDirectory`, which does **not** follow `Set-Location`. `-InstallDir .\bin` after a `cd` can silently land somewhere else. `~` is not expanded either, so `~\tools` becomes a literal `~` directory.

The PowerShell-correct call is:

`$ExecutionContext.SessionState.Path.GetUnresolvedProviderPathFromPSPath($Path)`

The default install dir is already absolute, so this only hits an explicit relative or tilde `-InstallDir`. Worth fixing.

## Architecture is process, not OS

`PROCESSOR_ARCHITECTURE` / `PROCESSOR_ARCHITEW6432` describe the **process**. An x64 PowerShell on ARM64 Windows can report AMD64 and install the amd64 zip on an ARM64 machine.

Soph’s alternative — `[Runtime.InteropServices.RuntimeInformation]::OSArchitecture` — asks the OS. ARM64 Windows has .NET 4.7.1+, so that should be available. The CI Verification section is x64-only, so the arm64 branch is still unproven. Easy to switch the API; confirming on real ARM64 hardware is a separate check.

## The “Added to PATH” message uses the wrong predicate

`$pathCommands.Count -eq 0` answers “is **any** `entire` on PATH?”, not “is the **install dir** on PATH?”.

If the directory is already in the user registry PATH but not this process’s `$env:Path`, you print “Added … to your user PATH” without adding anything, plus a restart hint — even though `Add-ToUserPath` just mutated `$env:Path` in-process.

The predicate should be `Test-PathContains -PathValue $env:Path -Directory $resolvedInstallDir` (and probably whether the registry entry was newly written). Small, clear bug.

## `entire.io/install.ps1` is not wired

Soph hit it live: `entire.io/install.sh` 307s to raw `main`; `entire.io/install.ps1` 307s to `/login?next=/install.ps1` and returns an HTML login page.

The README therefore uses the raw GitHub URL. That has two costs:

1. `scripts/install.ps1` and the `main` branch name become a public contract in three places (including `install.sh`’s Windows error text).
2. Anyone who guesses the `.sh` naming convention pipes HTML into `iex`.

Fixing the redirect is **not** this repo — it is the entire.io site/CDN. Until that exists, we should keep the raw URL, and maybe warn in the README that `entire.io/install.ps1` is not live yet. Once it is, switch the snippets.

## CI `-Help` does not catch any of this

Both Windows CI steps only run `-Help`, which returns at the first statement of `Install-Entire`. No arch detection, checksum matching, path normalization, or PATH logic.

The helpers (`Assert-Checksum`, `Test-PathContains`, `Get-NormalizedPath`, `Get-PlatformArchitecture`) are pure and Pester-testable, but they live inside the `& { }` wrapper that keeps `irm | iex` from leaking into the caller. That is a real tradeoff, not an accident — and it is exactly why the ordering bug survived.

Options: extract those helpers into a testable module, or add a `-SelfTest` / Pester job that dotsources under a test flag. Worth deciding; not blocking the PATH reorder.

## Nits from the review body (no threads)

- Commented-out nightly line inside the Windows copy-paste fence at README:71 looks like a leftover; the same command is already in the channels list.
- Neither web call passes `-TimeoutSec`, so a hung connection hangs forever.

---

**What I would do in this PR:** reorder PATH vs conflict check (blocker), fix `Get-NormalizedPath`, fix the PATH success predicate, drop or uncomment the README leftover, add `-TimeoutSec`. Architecture: switch to `OSArchitecture` unless we have a reason not to.

**Needs a call from you:**

1. `entire.io/install.ps1` redirect — this PR, a follow-up on the site, or leave the raw URL and document it?
2. How far to go on tests — Pester for the pure helpers in this PR, or leave CI as parse-only for now?
3. ARM64 — change the API now, or wait until someone can run it on ARM64 hardware?

If you want, I can start with the three installer bugs that do not need those answers.
Lets talk one by one. give me the feedback list

Soph’s open items, in review order:

1. **PATH update vs conflict throw** — `Add-ToUserPath` runs after the throw, so the documented nightly + Scoop path never completes and rerunning does not help.
2. **`-InstallDir` path normalization** — `[IO.Path]::GetFullPath` ignores PowerShell `cd` in 5.1 and does not expand `~`.
3. **Architecture detection** — `PROCESSOR_ARCHITECTURE` is the process, not the OS (x64 PowerShell on ARM64 Windows).
4. **“Added to PATH” predicate** — `$pathCommands.Count -eq 0` is “any `entire` on PATH”, not “install dir on PATH”.
5. **`entire.io/install.ps1` redirect** — that URL is not wired; it returns an HTML login page.
6. **CI only runs `-Help`** — no coverage of arch, checksum, path, or PATH logic.

Nits from the review body (no threads):

7. **Commented-out nightly line** in the Windows README copy-paste fence.
8. **No `-TimeoutSec`** on the web calls.

Which one first?
1. what would you propose to fix it ?
I’ll check how `install.sh` handles the same PATH-conflict case so the proposal matches that intent.

**Do not check PATH until after we have installed the files and updated PATH.** That is the whole bug: we abort using a snapshot taken while Scoop still wins, so `Add-ToUserPath` never runs.

`install.sh` already copies first, then looks at `command -v entire`. It cannot fix PATH itself, so a later foreign binary is a hard error. The Windows installer *can* prepend the user PATH, so it should do that, then re-evaluate.

Proposed order for the archive path (nightly, or stable without Scoop):

1. Download, verify, copy (keep that as-is).
2. Unless `-NoPathUpdate`: put `$resolvedInstallDir` **first** on both the user registry PATH and `$env:Path`.
3. Re-run `Get-EntireOnPath` (do not reuse the earlier snapshot).
4. First hit is ours → warn about any other `entire` still on PATH; do not throw.
5. First hit is still not ours → throw.

With `-NoPathUpdate`, skip step 2 and throw if something else wins, and say that PATH was left unchanged because of the flag.

One extra detail: today’s `Add-ToUserPath` only prepends if the directory is **absent**. If `~\.local\bin` is already on PATH but **after** Scoop, it is a no-op and the throw still fires. The helper should **move the directory to the front** when it is already present later in the list.

I would **not** call `Add-ToUserPath` before the copy. That writes the user PATH even if checksum or extract fails. Soph’s “move it above the conflict check” is the right *relative* order; the check itself should move to **after** the install, which is where PATH update already lives.

That should make the documented nightly + Scoop path succeed on the first run.

content.text:
Your log is a successful **warn-only** run. It is not the case Soph is talking about.

What your output shows:

- Check ran **after** the copy (`Entire CLI installed to …`, then `Installed to:`). That matches `18f7d5c19`, not current HEAD. HEAD moved the check **before** download and says `Install destination:`.
- It printed **both** binaries and “takes priority”, so the **first** `entire` on PATH was already `C:\Users\Victor\.local\bin\entire.exe`. Scoop was second. No throw.

Soph’s case is a **first** nightly install where `~\.local\bin` is **not** on PATH yet. Then `Get-Command` only sees Scoop, `$firstIsOurs` is false, and the script throws **before** `Add-ToUserPath`. A rerun does the same thing.

On your machine, `.local\bin` was already **ahead of** `scoop\shims` — previous installer run, a new terminal after PATH was written, or you added it yourself. That is why you got the friendly warning instead of the throw.

Quick check in that same session:

```powershell
($env:Path -split ';') | Select-String 'local\\bin|scoop\\shims'
Get-Command entire -All | Format-Table Source
```

If `.local\bin` is listed first, you did not hit Soph’s path.

To reproduce his bug: a shell where `.local\bin` is **absent** from `$env:Path` and the user PATH, Scoop’s `entire` still resolves, then `.\scripts\install.ps1 -Channel nightly`. On current HEAD that should error during the pre-copy check, with no download.

tell me why we are calling Add-ToUserPath after checking if entire on path? I've got it working because the install path was already on user's path env, because otherwise, we copy the binary, we check if it is not there and then fail without adding install into path. Why do we do that?

There is no Windows-specific reason. The order was copied from `install.sh`, where it makes sense. Here it does not.

**Unix (`install.sh`)** cannot write your shell PATH. Flow is: copy the binary, then `command -v entire`.

- Nothing on PATH → print “add this to `.zshrc`” and exit 0.
- Something else wins → error. The user must delete the old binary or edit PATH. The script cannot do that for them.

**Windows** *can* prepend the user PATH (`Add-ToUserPath`). The script still used the Unix sequence: inspect PATH **as it is now**, and only call `Add-ToUserPath` if that inspection did not throw.

So `Add-ToUserPath` was written as a helper for the **empty** case (`pathCommands.Count -eq 0` → “Added … to your user PATH”). It was **not** used to *resolve* “Scoop is already first,” which is the normal machine if you followed the stable docs.

The fail-closed idea is: don’t tell the user nightly is installed if `entire` still hits Scoop. That part is right. The mistake is treating “Scoop is first **before we prepend**” as a user error. On this installer, prepending **is** the fix. Checking first, then throwing, skips the only step that would make our binary win.

That is why it worked on your box: `.local\bin` was already first, so the check saw “ours” and never threw, then `Add-ToUserPath` ran (or no-op’d). On a machine where that directory is missing from PATH, copy succeeds, check sees only Scoop, throw, PATH never updated.

Correct order: copy → prepend (unless `-NoPathUpdate`) → look at PATH again → warn if others remain, throw only if we still lose.
can you fix it?
I’ll reorder PATH update before the conflict check, and make `Add-ToUserPath` move the install dir to the front when it’s already later on PATH.
I'll prepend the install dir (move-to-front if it's already later on PATH), then re-check conflicts so we don't throw before PATH is updated.

what is this doing? 
        $userPath = [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("Path", "User")
        $userPathChanged = $false
        if (-not (Test-PathIsFirst -PathValue $userPath -Directory $Directory)) {
            $newUserPath = Get-PathWithDirectoryFirst -PathValue $userPath -Directory $Directory

That block writes the **persistent** user PATH (the one new terminals inherit), not this process’s `$env:Path`.

1. **Read** the user’s PATH from the registry (`Path` for the current user).
2. **If** `$Directory` is already the **first** entry, do nothing (`$userPathChanged` stays `$false`).
3. **Otherwise** rebuild PATH with that directory in front (add it, or move it if it was later in the list), **write it back** to the user environment, and set `$userPathChanged = $true`.

`$userPathChanged` is what drives the “Added … to your user PATH” message. The in-session update is the later `$env:Path = …` so *this* shell can find `entire` immediately.

lets go thru this one next:
[IO.Path]::GetFullPath resolves relative paths against [Environment]::CurrentDirectory, which Windows PowerShell 5.1 does not keep in sync with Set-Location — so -InstallDir .\bin after a cd silently installs somewhere else. ~\tools is worse: ~ isn't expanded, so you get a literal ~ directory.

tell me the context. is it true?
I’ll check how `-InstallDir` is resolved in the script and confirm the 5.1 `GetFullPath` / `cd` behavior Soph describes.

**Yes. Soph is right.** It is a real 5.1 quirk, and it only matters for an explicit `-InstallDir`.

**Where it lives.** Direct (non-Scoop) installs do:

```393:394:scripts/install.ps1
        $resolvedInstallDir = Get-NormalizedPath -Path $SelectedInstallDir
        $installPath = Join-Path $resolvedInstallDir "entire.exe"
```

`Get-NormalizedPath` is `[IO.Path]::GetFullPath`, then strip a trailing `\` (except for `C:\`). Same helper is used by `Test-SamePath` to compare PATH entries.

**Default path is already absolute.** `-InstallDir` defaults to `Join-Path $HOME ".local\bin"` → `C:\Users\Victor\.local\bin`. `GetFullPath` on that does not use the current directory. Documented one-liners never pass `-InstallDir`.

**What breaks.** Someone runs:

```powershell
cd C:\work
.\scripts\install.ps1 -Channel nightly -InstallDir .\bin
```

or `-InstallDir ~\tools`.

- **`.\bin` on Windows PowerShell 5.1:** `Set-Location` / `cd` updates `$PWD`. It does **not** reliably update `[Environment]::CurrentDirectory`. `GetFullPath` uses that process directory, so the zip can land in `{where powershell started}\bin`, not `C:\work\bin`. PowerShell 7 usually keeps them in sync, so this is a 5.1 bug (and 5.1 is a stated target).
- **`~\tools`:** `~` is a PowerShell home alias, not a .NET path. `GetFullPath` treats it as a folder named `~`, e.g. `C:\work\~\tools`.

**Soph’s replacement** — `$ExecutionContext.SessionState.Path.GetUnresolvedProviderPathFromPSPath($Path)` — is the usual PowerShell way: resolve against `$PWD`, expand `~`, and do not require the path to exist yet (`New-Item` creates it later). “Unresolved” here means “don’t demand it already exists,” not “leave it relative.”

**Worth keeping after that:** still canonicalize and trim trailing `\` (the rest of `Get-NormalizedPath`). A solid shape is PS-path first, then `GetFullPath` on the now-absolute result so `.` / `..` collapse and `CurrentDirectory` is irrelevant.
so, what do y propose to fix it ?

Change **`Get-NormalizedPath` only**. Every caller already goes through it (`-InstallDir` and `Test-SamePath`), so Scoop shims and PATH entries keep working.

Resolve with PowerShell first, then let .NET canonicalize:

```powershell
function Get-NormalizedPath {
    param([string] $Path)

    $fullPath = [IO.Path]::GetFullPath(
        $ExecutionContext.SessionState.Path.GetUnresolvedProviderPathFromPSPath($Path)
    )
    # existing drive-root + TrimEnd logic unchanged
    ...
}
```

- `GetUnresolvedProviderPathFromPSPath` uses `$PWD` and expands `~`.
- `GetFullPath` on that **absolute** result collapses `.` / `..` and no longer consults `[Environment]::CurrentDirectory`.

Do **not** special-case `-InstallDir`. The default is already absolute; relative and tilde are the only cases that change.

I would not add a new parameter or a second helper. After this, `-InstallDir .\bin` after `cd` and `-InstallDir ~\tools` install where a PowerShell user expects.
where a powershell expects it ?

Wherever PowerShell itself would treat as the location of that path **right now** — `$PWD` plus `~`, not the process’s leftover working directory.

Examples, after `cd C:\work`:

| You pass | 5.1 today (`GetFullPath`) | After the fix |
|---|---|---|
| *(omit `-InstallDir`)* | `C:\Users\Victor\.local\bin` | same |
| `-InstallDir .\bin` | `{where powershell.exe started}\bin` (often `C:\Users\Victor\bin`) | `C:\work\bin` |
| `-InstallDir ~\tools` | `C:\work\~\tools` (a folder literally named `~`) | `C:\Users\Victor\tools` |
| `-InstallDir C:\apps\entire` | `C:\apps\entire` | same |

“Where PowerShell expects it” means: same as `Set-Location` / tab-completion / `mkdir .\bin`, not `[Environment]::CurrentDirectory`.

Next open thread is architecture detection. I’ll pull Soph’s comment and the current `Get-PlatformArchitecture` code so we can judge it the same way.

This is Soph’s **architecture** thread (`Get-PlatformArchitecture`).

**What the script does.** It picks the zip from env vars:

- `PROCESSOR_ARCHITEW6432` if set (classic: 32-bit process on a 64-bit OS)
- else `PROCESSOR_ARCHITECTURE`

Those describe the **process**, not the machine. The comment even says W6432 is for a 32-bit PowerShell. That misses the case Soph cares about.

**The case.** x64 PowerShell on ARM64 Windows (very common: `powershell.exe` from a shortcut, VS, some terminals). Then:

- `PROCESSOR_ARCHITECTURE` = `AMD64`
- `PROCESSOR_ARCHITEW6432` is usually **unset** (x64 is not WOW64-32)
